title: Designing a URL shortener

facts.text: The service must create a unique short alias for a URL, redirect visitors to the original URL, and expire links after a default timespan, with high availability and minimal latency; preventing abuse and recording analytics are extended requirements.

After checking scale assumptions with the interviewer, assume a read-heavy 100:1 read/write ratio and 100 million links generated per month: about 40 URLs per second written and 4000 redirections per second.
Taking each request and each stored record as about 500 bytes, incoming bandwidth is 20 KB/second, outgoing is about 2 MB/second, and 12 billion records kept for 10 years need around 6 TB.
By the 80/20 rule, caching 20% of the 350M redirection requests per day needs around 35GB of memory per day.

Two tables suffice at first: users (name, email, createdAt) and URLs (expiration, hash, originalURL, creator's userID), with the hash column indexed. Data that is not strongly relational suits NoSQL such as DynamoDB, Cassandra or MongoDB.
Create URL takes an API key, the original URL and an optional expiration and returns the short URL; Get URL maps a short URL back to the original; Delete URL returns a boolean result.
The API key prevents abuse: it lets the service limit each user to a certain number of requests per second or minute, a standard practice for developer APIs.

Base62 (A-Z, a-z, 0-9) gives about 3.5 trillion 7-character keys (62^7), and MD5 hashing the URL yields 32 hex digits to make one. Both risk duplicates and collisions, and recomputing hashes adds overhead.

A counter encoded in base62 is a single point of failure, and several counters collide; ZooKeeper can hand each server a range such as 1 to 1,000,000, which guarantees non-duplicate keys, and can itself run in several instances.

A standalone Key Generation Service creates unique keys ahead of time in a separate database; used keys move to another table under locking so concurrent servers never share one, and some keys are kept in memory.
To create a URL, the API server gets a unique key from the Key Generation Service, which marks it used; the server writes the entry to the database and cache and returns HTTP 201 (Created).
To access a URL, the API server checks the cache first, falls back to the database and issues an HTTP 301 (Redirect) to the original URL, or sends HTTP 404 (Not found) if the key is missing.

To scale out the database, partition it horizontally (sharding) by hash, list, range or composite schemes, and use consistent hashing to fix the uneven data and load distribution these can still cause.

Redis or Memcached servers beside the API server cache 20% of daily traffic with Least Recently Used eviction, which discards the least recently used key first; on a cache miss the servers read the database and update the cache.

Expired links can be removed by active cleanup, a lightweight cron-like service that periodically deletes them from storage and cache, or by passive cleanup, a lazy removal when a user accesses an expired link.

To remove single points of failure, run multiple instances of the servers and Key Generation Service, put load balancers between components, add read replicas for the database, a standby replica for the key database, and a replicated cache.

notes: The source's KGS key-storage estimate is inconsistent (300 GB in one sentence, ~390 GB in its formula, and 6 x 56.8 billion is neither), so that estimate is not used as a fact (sents 77c6363ffeed, 1eb3de12ed3a). Security (private URLs, HTTP 401) and per-URL analytics are left out for the 16-fact cap.

definition.text: URL shortening makes a long URL substantially shorter while it still leads to the same page, by using a redirect that points to the page with the long URL.

facts.text: A short URL saves space when sharing, is less likely to be mistyped, and lets links be tracked individually across devices.
A friendly short URL helps messaging technologies that limit message length, such as SMS, reduces typing when copying from print, is easier to remember, and can serve as a permalink.
The redirect instruction sent to the browser carries an HTTP status code such as 301 (moved permanently), 302 (found), 307 (temporary redirect) or 308 (permanent redirect).
Shortening services give detailed click statistics, which can be simpler than setting up an equally powerful server-side analytics engine and need no access to the server.
Typically data: and javascript: URLs are not supported, for security reasons, to combat attacks like cross-site scripting and session hijacking.

definition.text: A shortening service ties each long URL to a unique key, the part after the domain name, that it builds from letters and digits.

facts.text: Keys are case-sensitive most of the time, so using the wrong case may lead to a different destination URL.
Keys can be written in base 36 (26 letters and 10 numbers) or, when upper and lower case differ, in base 62 (26 + 26 + 10).
A hash function can form the key, or a random number can be generated so that the key sequence is not predictable.
Users may propose their own custom keys, such as shortening a long product URL to a readable name.

definition.text: Short URLs add a layer of complexity to retrieving pages and bring abuse, linkrot and privacy risks.

facts.text: Every access needs at least one more DNS lookup (possibly cached) and one more HTTP/HTTPS request, which adds latency and the risk of failure if the shortening service becomes unavailable.
Short URLs suffer linkrot: if the shortening service stops working, all URLs it issued become broken.
A short URL hides the target address, so it can redirect to unexpected or malicious sites and bypass site blocklists; some websites prevent short redirected URLs from being posted.
Browsers do not resend POST bodies when a redirect is encountered, an operational limit of shortening services.

definition.text: Some providers let a shortened URL expire after a set time, on a certain date, or after a number of uses.

facts.text: A permanent URL is not necessarily good: obsolete short URLs stay in circulation long after they stop pointing to a relevant destination, which has security implications.
A short-lived URL suits a one-off access or file download that is no longer needed within a couple of minutes.
A Microsoft Security Brief recommends creating short-lived URLs, for security reasons rather than convenience.
Providers who claim short URLs never expire may still discontinue the service at any time.

definition.text: Base62 writes numbers with 62 symbols: the capital letters A-Z, the lower case letters a-z and the digits 0-9.

facts.text: A key of N Base62 characters can name 62^N different URLs, so each added character multiplies the key space by 62.
Base62 output [a-zA-Z0-9] suits URLs because no special characters need escaping, while Base 64 adds + and / characters that cause issues for URLs.
Base62 is deterministic, with no randomness: one input number or hash always gives the same encoded string.
